sentences.text: The meeting reviewed the conceptual design of a universal TV remote control, addressing market research findings regarding user preferences for fashion, innovation, and ease of use.
The team discussed specific design features including a flip-top mechanism, kinetic charging, and a combination of LCD and rubber buttons to minimize repetitive strain injury (RSI).
Decisions were reached on the internal components and general aesthetic direction, while voice recognition was tentatively included pending cost verification.
Participant A noted that the previous meeting's agenda was postponed due to a need for more information, and the group agreed to proceed with the industrial design presentation first.
Participant D presented a working design concept for a device that sends signals to change TV states, noting that most current remotes use infrared and are powered by bulky triple-A batteries.
Participant B questioned whether the triple-A batteries were the source of the bulkiness, and Participant D confirmed that the size is due to the batteries required to fit them.
Participant D proposed looking at smaller battery options or other power sources to reduce the size of the control, suggesting a design that is easy to carry and less likely to be lost.
Participant B highlighted that market research found 75% of users dislike the look and feel of current remotes, with 80% willing to spend more for a fancy design.
Participant B reported findings that 50% of users only use 10% of the buttons on their remotes, leading to frustration with lost controls and repetitive strain injury (RSI).
Participant B mentioned that younger age groups (35 and under) preferred LCD screens and speech recognition, while older age groups did not.
Participant A clarified that the new project requirements exclude teletext and combined controls, limiting the device to TV and Video Plus functions.

Participant D suggested that incorporating speech recognition might be too expensive and not very effective, while Participant B noted that a substantial number of older respondents were 'don't knows' regarding new technology.
Participant A proposed a beeping alarm on the TV itself as a cheaper alternative to a keychain whistle or speech recognition for locating the remote.
The team decided to use a kinetic charging system with a small watch-type battery instead of standard triple-A batteries.
The design was finalized as a flip-top model with a plastic body and a rubberized cover.
The interface was decided to feature an LCD screen on the top flip section and rubberized buttons on the bottom section.
The aesthetic direction was set to use fruit and vegetable colors for the rubber cover, avoiding specific fruit or shell shapes to remain non-tacky.
The team agreed to incorporate voice recognition software into the design, pending further cost verification.
The company logo was decided to be incorporated into the design, potentially as an engraving or inset, without interfering with the overall look.
Participant B will look at functional requirements from the marketing point of view and may email extra details if needed.
Participant A will email any remaining questions until the team is fully connected.
Participant D will present the prototype and the look and feel design.

The team will evaluate the prototype against the criteria (fancy look, technological innovation, ease of use, RSI minimization, location features) using a seven-point scale to determine consensus ratings.
Financial feasibility will be checked for voice recognition and the beeper function to decide on final inclusion.
